Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and ate. And after speaking until daybreak, he departed.

c: is a key word in the Bible. It is used to indicate God’s kindness and favor, often in terms of salvation to the undeserving. The New Testament stresses that grace came through Jesus Christ (
). This is not to say that God’s grace was not active in the Old Testament; rather, God’s gracious activity toward humanity reached its culmination through his Son.
According to the book of Acts, God’s great favor was initially experienced in the Jewish community (see
); later, it became clear that God’s grace in Jesus Christ extends to Gentiles as well (
). Signs and wonders attested the reality of God’s grace at work among the Gentiles (
Paul proclaimed the Good News “about the wonderful grace of God” (
). Paul never seeks to prove that God is gracious, but he assumes it as a fact when he presents the Good News (see, e.g.,
). Paul rules out any idea that we merit our salvation, because God acts solely by his grace (
). Our good works do not give us right standing with God—if they did, God would be obliged to reward us for our efforts, just as a worker earns a wage (see
God’s grace continues to impact believers throughout their lives—not just in the moment of conversion. Second Peter closes with a command for Christians to “grow in the grace” of Jesus Christ (
). Paul encouraged Christians to “continue to rely on the grace of God” as they remained faithful to their Lord (
). And when Paul left the Ephesian elders, he commended them “to God and the message of his grace,” the divine message that was able to build them up and sustain them (

). God’s grace is at the core of the Christian message and the Christian experience, from beginning to end. It is no wonder that the theme of grace is so prevalent in the writings of Jesus’ early followers.
